Background/objectives: Conventional polymethyl methacrylate denture base resins exhibit limitations in mechanical durability and microbial resistance. Zein-coated magnesium oxide nanoparticles (zMgO NPs) have previously demonstrated antimicrobial activity when incorporated into dental polymers. However, their influence on mechanical performance has not been thoroughly characterized. This study investigated whether integrating zMgO NPs affects the flexural strength of heat-polymerized and autopolymerizing acrylic denture base materials. Methods: Five commercially available polymethyl methacrylate resins (three heat-cured and two self-cured) were evaluated. Sixty samples of each type were randomly assigned to four groups based on nanoparticle concentration: 0%, 0.3%, 0.5%, and 1% by weight. Sample fabrication and testing were performed in accordance with ISO 20795-1 for denture base polymers. Flexural strength was assessed using a three-point bending test. Data were analyzed using two-way analysis of variance followed by post hoc comparisons with statistical significance set at 0.05. Results: Samples containing 0.5% and 1% zMgO NPs demonstrated significantly higher flexural strength than controls, whereas the 0.3% zMgO NPs groups showed no statistically significant difference compared to the control. Conclusions: Incorporation of zMgO NPs maintains the flexural performance of denture base polymers. Higher nanoparticle loadings produced significantly higher flexural strength, suggesting potential for multifunctional denture materials with improved structural durability. Future work should include longterm aging and simulated oral conditions to confirm clinical applicability.

## Introduction

Edentulism remains a prevalent condition worldwide, particularly among older adults, and is associated with functional, nutritional, and psychosocial consequences (1). Removable dentures continue to be a common treatment option for restoring oral function in edentulous patients, particularly when circumstances don’t allow for a fixed prosthesis (2). Among available denture base polymers, polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) is the most frequently selected material in clinical prosthodontics due to its balance of handling characteristics, affordability, and biological compatibility (3). It is the key component in both heat-cured and self-cured acrylic resins, which are used in denture base manufacturing and denture repair (4, 5). It has remained the dominant material because it combines clinical compatibility with practical manufacturability and economic accessibility (6, 7).

Despite its widespread use, PMMA prostheses remain susceptible to structural and biological limitations. These include brittleness, fatigue-related degradation, dimensional changes during polymerization, and surface properties that may facilitate microbial accumulation. Such weaknesses contribute to fracture risk, particularly along stress-prone regions such as the midline, where cyclic loading and material fatigue can lead to failure over time (8, 9). Fractures can develop from functional stresses, user habits, denture handling, resin porosity, thin areas within denture bases, and crack formation (10, 11). John et al. reported that 68% of acrylic denture base failures happen within 3 years of manufacturing, mainly due to deformation from masticatory loads, leading to fatigue fractures (12). Another major limitation is the reduced mechanical durability of repaired denture bases, which contributes to a shorter interval to re-fracture incidents and increased patient visits and costs (13–15).

Microbial colonization of denture surfaces is another clinically relevant concern. Biofilm accumulation beneath prostheses has been strongly associated with denture stomatitis, an inflammatory condition affecting mucosal tissues. This condition is common among denture wearers and is influenced by hygiene practices, prosthesis fit, systemic health status, and medication use. Candida species, especially Candida albicans, are frequently implicated in its development (16). The condition is very common, with studies showing a prevalence of 15%–80% among denture wearers worldwide (17–19).

Efforts to improve denture base performance have increasingly focused on nanoscale reinforcement approaches, as nanomaterials can alter polymer behavior through interfacial interactions that influence stress transfer, chain mobility, and surface characteristics. However, their effectiveness depends strongly on particle composition, concentration, and dispersion within the host material (13, 14, 20–25). Azmy et al. previously investigated the mechanical performance of modifying PMMA acrylic resin with 3% and 7% zirconium dioxide, silicon dioxide, and titanium dioxide nanoparticles. Their study concluded that zirconium dioxide improved PMMA’s flexural and impact strength at both concentrations, while silicon dioxide, and titanium dioxide only showed improvement at low concentrations (22).

Ideally, the addition of the nanoparticles should improve or maintain the inherent esthetics, biocompatibility, mechanical strength, and dimensional stability of the acrylic resin (26). The lack of a standardized consensus on evaluation protocols and biological implications complicates the selection of nanoparticles. It is therefore crucial that the selected nano-fillers demonstrate not only functional and mechanical benefits but also biological safety and biocompatibility.

Magnesium oxide nanoparticles (MgO NPs) have recently been popularized as a reinforcement for different dental materials (27, 28). However, their performance depends on achieving stable dispersion, since particle clustering can reduce functional surface area and limit reinforcement efficiency (29). Surface modification strategies have therefore been developed to enhance stability within polymer matrices (30). This is achieved through zein, a natural protein-based polymer that constitutes approximately 50%–70% of the endosperm protein in corn (31). It is frequently used for various textile, food, and pharmaceutical indications (32). Its use as a carrier is costeffective and allows for efficient utilization of by-products (33). When incorporated with nanoparticles, this polymer can be used as a coating, limiting hydrophobic interactions and stabilizing the surface tension that arises from a lack of atoms available to bond to the nanoparticles (32, 33). Zein has successfully been used with MgO NPs to provide antimicrobial benefits (34, 35).

Previous investigations have demonstrated that zein-coated magnesium oxide nanoparticles (zMgO NPs) confer strong antimicrobial effects when incorporated into dental materials (36–39). The significance of adding an antimicrobial effect to acrylic resin denture bases is especially important, as a denture resistant to Candida albicans may help lower the occurrence of denture stomatitis (16).

Although the biological benefits of this nanoparticle system have been reported, its influence on the mechanical performance of PMMA denture base polymers has not been fully characterized. In particular, limited information exists regarding how varying concentrations of zMgO NPs affect flexural strength, a critical property governing clinical longevity. The present study aimed to address this gap by evaluating the impact of adding zMgO NPs at concentrations of 0.0%, 0.3%, 0.5%, and 1.0% on the flexural strength of various types of PMMA-based denture base resins. The null hypothesis was that there were no significant differences in flexural strength among the different types of acrylic resin at all nanoparticle concentrations.

## Methodology

## Materials

Five commercially available PMMA denture base materials were evaluated, including three heat-polymerized resins (ProBase Hot, Ivoclar Vivadent, Schaan, Liechtenstein; Vertex Heat-Cured, Vertex Dental, Soesterberg, The Netherlands; DPI Heat-Cure, Dental Products of India, Fort, Mumbai) and two autopolymerizing formulations (Vertex Self-Cured, Vertex Dental, Soesterberg, The Netherlands; GC Nature-Cryl Pour, GC

This study employed a balanced 5 × 4 factorial design with 5 acrylic resin types and 4 nanoparticle concentrations (0%, 0.3%, 0.5%, and 1%), yielding 20 experimental groups. Using G*Power (Version 3.1.9.6), assuming an effect size of f = 0.25, a significance level of 0.05, and 80% power, a minimum total sample size of 289 samples was required (40). To ensure adequate power and maintain equal group sizes, 300 samples were included, corresponding to 15 samples in each of the 20 experimental groups (Figure 1). Samples were first prepared according to the assigned acrylic resin type. Within each acrylic resin type, samples were randomly assigned to one of four zMgO NP concentration groups (0%, 0.3%, 0.5%, or 1%) using a computer-generated random number sequence to ensure unbiased allocation to the nanoparticle concentration groups.

## Preparation of nanoparticles

Portions of the nanoparticle synthesis procedure were adapted from our previously published work (34, 35). MgO NPs were produced through a controlled precipitation and thermal

conversion approach. The magnesium acetate precursor solution (6.44 g with 75 mL of distilled water, dissolved for 30 min at 25 °C) was combined with urea (1.2 g with 25 mL of distilled water), subjected to autoclaving (15 min), and subsequently purified through centrifugation and filtration steps. The resulting product was dried (60 °C for 24 h) and calcined (600 ° C for 1 h) to obtain crystalline MgO particles.

Surface stabilization was achieved using the zein coating (32–34, 41). The polymer (0.02 g) was dissolved in alkaline ethanol and added dropwise to a polyvinyl alcohol dispersion (15 mL of 0.9% w/v) containing MgO (0.02 g) at 10 °C, with ultrasonic shear applied to promote uniform coating (20 kHz, 750 W). The suspension was stirred to allow solvent evaporation (500 rpm, room temp), purified by centrifugation (300 rpm, 45 min), suspended in buffer (5 mL), and lyophilized following the addition of a cryoprotectant (2% w/v trehalose).

## Flexural strength test

To assess flexural strength in accordance with ISO 20795-1, a 3-point bending test was conducted on a universal testing machine (Instron 5944, Instron 5000 Premier Testing Systems series, Instron® Mechanical Testing Systems). The samples were loaded onto the machine and tested at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/ min using a 50 kN loading cell, with the support span length set to 50 mm (45). ## Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (Version 23, IBM Corp., Armonk, USA). Two-way ANOVA was used to evaluate the effects of acrylic resin type and nanoparticle concentration on flexural strength. When significant differences were identified, post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Tukey’s test. The level of statistical significance was set at 0.05.

## Results

Two-way ANOVA demonstrated a statistically significant effect of acrylic resin type on flexural strength (p < 0.05; p = 0.025). Across all materials, a consistent concentrationdependent increase in flexural strength was observed with increasing zMgO NPs content (Figure 2 and Table 2). No statistically significant differences were identified between the control samples and those containing 0.3% zMgO NPs for any of the tested materials (p > 0.05 for all groups; ProBase HC: p = 0.32; DPI HC: p = 0.07; Vertex HC: p = 0.36; GC SC: p = 0.77; Vertex SC: p = 0.22).

In contrast, incorporation of 0.5% zMgO NPs resulted in statistically significant increases in flexural strength compared to controls across all acrylic resin types (p < 0.05 for all groups; Probase HC: p = 0.01; DPI HC: p = 0.007; Vertex HC: p = 0.02;

GC SC: p = 0.04; Vertex SC: p = 0.008). Similarly, the 1% zMgO NPs group had a statistically significant increase in flexural strength compared to the controls across all acrylic resin types (p < 0.05 for all groups; Probase HC: p = 0.008; DPI HC: p = 0.0026; Vertex HC: p = 0.003; GC SC: p = 0.000; Vertex SC: p = 0.002).

Pairwise comparisons between nanoparticle concentrations further confirmed this trend. Samples containing 0.5% and 1% zMgO NPs demonstrated significantly higher flexural strength than those containing 0.3% across all materials (p < 0.05). Additionally, 1% zMgO NPs produced significantly higher flexural strength compared to 0.5% in all groups (p < 0.05), indicating a progressive, concentration-dependent reinforcement effect.

## Discussion

Edentulism continues to represent a prevalent clinical condition, particularly in aging populations, and prosthetic rehabilitation frequently relies on acrylic resin–based dentures. Although PMMA remains the standard denture base material, mechanical failure is a persistent clinical concern. Fracture events are multifactorial and can result from cyclic masticatory loading, structural design limitations, material fatigue, and accidental trauma (46). Previous reinforcement strategies have attempted to improve mechanical behavior through chemical modification of the polymer matrix, including crosslinking or rubber copolymerization. While such approaches may enhance impact resistance, they may also adversely affect other mechanical parameters such as flexural strength and fatigue resistance, highlighting the difficulty of optimizing multiple properties simultaneously (20, 47).

The inclusion of nanoparticles in denture bases has been increasingly studied over the last decade. These nanoparticles can either be incorporated into denture base resin during mixing or utilized as coatings on the intaglio surface of the prosthesis to minimize microbial attachment and biofilm development (7, 48). Depending on formulation characteristics, the fillers may restrict polymer mobility, redistribute applied stress, and improve resistance to deformation (20, 26, 49). For metal oxide nanoparticles, both the concentration and size must be adequately low to ensure homogeneous mixtures (50, 51). Uniform dispersion is especially important because aggregation can produce stress concentration sites that compromise structural integrity (52).

In the present study, low concentrations of zMgO NPs were selected because these levels (0%, 0.3%, 0.5%, and 1%) previously demonstrated antimicrobial activity while maintaining material stability (35). Earlier investigations using similar nanoparticle systems reported significant reductions in microbial adhesion without evidence of particle leaching, suggesting stable incorporation within the polymer matrix (37). Additionally, we previously found that Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed that surface coatings helped achieve more uniform nanoparticle dispersion and reduce agglomeration, thereby improving interfacial bonding between the filler and the polymer matrix. Moreover, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy analyses detected changes in peak intensity patterns after nanoparticle incorporation, indicating interaction between inorganic fillers and resin components (34, 37, 53).

It is important to highlight that heat-cured denture base materials are subjected to high heat and pressure, which leads to extended polymer chains, lower levels of residual monomer, and better degrees of monomer conversion. In contrast, autopolymerizing denture base materials typically contain excess monomers that can interact with the inorganic nanoparticles, leading to increased peak heights and variations in peak intensity (5, 7).

Meanwhile, zein is a completely amorphous polymer that exhibits plasticizing viscoelasticity and a glass transition temperature of about 165 °C, although this glass transition temperature decreases significantly as the degree of plasticization increases. Its degradation point is 270 °C, which is much higher than the polymerization temperature of the acrylic resin, which should never exceed 100 °C to avoid monomer evaporation at 100.3 °C (54–56).

Flexural forces occur during the everyday use of dentures, as they are subjected to repeated bending, flexing, and twisting. These forces can increase in the presence of different bone resorption patterns, creating an uneven landscape among the alveolar ridges. Therefore, denture bases must possess adequate flexural strength to extend their clinical viability (57). This may further be influenced by the chemical composition of the acrylic resin, the curing method, the degree of polymerization, and storage conditions (6, 7).

significant increase in strength compared to the unmodified acrylic groups. Therefore, the null hypothesis was rejected. The minimum flexural strength value of standard dental base polymers is mandated to be 65 MPa by the International Organization for Standardization ISO-20795-1 (9, 45, 58). All groups, both modified and unmodified, met this threshold. This pattern suggests a threshold effect in which reinforcement becomes measurable only once sufficient nanoparticle content is present to influence internal stress distribution. When nanoparticles are evenly distributed, they can act as barriers to crack propagation and reduce localized strain accumulation. At lower concentrations, particle spacing may be insufficient to produce measurable reinforcement, which could explain why statistically significant improvements were only detected at higher loading levels.

In this study, both heat-cured and self-cured acrylic resins were used to compare their effects. Heat-polymerized acrylic resins exhibited consistently higher flexural strength values compared to the autopolymerizing resins across all nanoparticle concentrations. The magnitude of improvement was more pronounced in heat-cured materials. Self-cured resins presented lower baseline values and smaller absolute gains, although a similar nanoparticle concentration-dependent trend was observed. This could be due to the inherent polymerization efficiency of heat-cured and self-cured acrylic resins. Heat-polymerized resins typically exhibit lower residual monomer content and a denser polymer network, which can contribute to improved mechanical performance and may enhance interfacial interactions with reinforcing agents such as nanoparticles (59, 60). Conversely, self-cured acrylic resins tend to exhibit higher porosity and residual monomer content due to their chemical polymerization mechanism, which can negatively affect their structural integrity and limit reinforcement efficiency (61, 62).

The findings highlight the importance of interfacial compatibility between nanofillers and polymer matrices. Reinforcement is not solely dependent on nanoparticle presence but on the efficiency of load transfer across the fillermatrix interface. Surface modification strategies that improve bonding may therefore be as critical as nanoparticle concentration in determining final mechanical performance. Moreover, from a clinical perspective, improved flexural strength may translate into enhanced resistance to midline fracture. Materials that maintain mechanical integrity under cyclic loading may reduce repair frequency, clinical chair time, and long-term costs for patients. Therefore, nanoparticlemodified denture bases could provide practical advantages beyond laboratory performance metrics.

The literature indicates that varying types and proportions of nanoparticles may enhance or diminish the flexural strength of acrylic resins. Ansarifard et al. reported a statistically significant increase in flexural strength when including 50 and 500 μg/mL copper oxide NPs in PMMA (63). Karci et al. investigated the change in flexural strength of different acrylic resins when adding Al2O3, SiO2, and TiO2 nanoparticles. There was an increase in flexural strength at 1% with the Al2O3 and TiO2 groups surpassing the SiO2 group, but a decrease at 3% and 5% with all nanoparticles (52). Alzayyat et al. incorporated 0.05%, 0.25%, 0.5%, and 1% SiO2 NPs with acrylic powder, and found

that the inclusion of the nanoparticles significantly increased the flexural strength, although the degree of increase significantly reduced with higher concentrations (23).

Similarly, Gad et al. prepared 0.25%, 0.5%, and 0.75% SiO2 NPs with acrylic denture bases and found a significant increase in the flexural strength of all groups (24). In another study, Gad investigated the effects of adding 0.5%, 1%, and 1.5% ZrO2 NPs and Ag NPs to heat-polymerized acrylic resin samples. The flexural strength significantly increased proportionally to the concentration of ZrO2 NPs, whereas the opposite effect was seen with the Ag NPs, with the flexural strength decreasing proportionally to the concentration of Ag NPs (21). Palaskar et al. assessed 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.3%, 0.4%, and 0.5% Ag NPs with heat-cured PMMA and found that flexural strength decreased as the percentage of Ag NPs increased, with the control group having the highest flexural strength (64). Albasarah et al. evaluated the effect of adding 2.5% and 5% ZrO2 NPs to PMMA denture bases on flexural strength at different material thicknesses. They concluded that the addition of the nanoparticles significantly improved flexural strength, even with reduced material thickness (65). Such discrepancies likely reflect differences in nanoparticle chemistry, concentration ranges, processing methods, and dispersion quality. These findings underscore the importance of optimizing formulation parameters rather than assuming uniform reinforcement effects across nanoparticle types.

Despite the promising attributes of nanoparticle-enhanced denture materials, several limitations should be considered. This study was conducted under in vitro conditions and did not fully replicate the complex intraoral environment, where denture base materials are subjected to thermal fluctuations, moisture, enzymatic activity, and cyclic masticatory loading. In addition, the present investigation focused solely on flexural strength, which, although clinically relevant, does not comprehensively represent the mechanical performance of denture base materials.

Future studies should include simulated oral conditions, including thermocycling, mechanical fatigue loading, and exposure to saliva, to better approximate clinical performance. Long-term investigations evaluating multiple mechanical and physical properties, such as impact strength, fracture toughness, fatigue resistance, and wear behavior, could reveal much on the durability of the nanoparticle-polymer interface. These future investigations are necessary to determine the translational potential and clinical applicability of these nanoparticle-modified denture materials.

## Conclusion

This study evaluated the effect of zMgO NPs on the flexural strength of PMMA denture bases to address the need for materials with improved mechanical and antimicrobial properties. The results demonstrated that incorporation of 0.5% and 1% zMgO NPs significantly increased flexural strength across multiple PMMA types. No significant improvement was observed at 0.3%, indicating a concentration-dependent effect. While these findings suggest that zMgO NPs could improve flexural strength, further research is needed to assess additional properties such as impact strength, fracture toughness, fatigue

# Evaluating Tolerance Levels of Dental Students in King Abdulaziz University, Saudi Arabia

**Authors:** Ghada H. Naguib; Abeer Alnowaiser; Jumana Mazhar; Mawadah Bahrawi; Alhassan K. Alsaiari; Abdulghani Mira; Roaa Abuljadayel; Mohamed T. Hamed

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Restorative Dentistry, Faculty of Dentistry King Abdulaziz University Jeddah Saudi Arabia | 2 Department of Oral Biology Cairo University School of Dentistry Cairo Egypt | 3 Department of Pediatric Dentistry, Faculty of Dentistry King Abdulaziz University Jeddah Saudi Arabia | 4 King Abdulaziz University Jeddah Saudi Arabia | 5 Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Prosthodontics, Faculty of Dentistry King Abdulaziz University Jeddah Saudi Arabia | 6 Department of Fixed Prosthodontics Cairo University School of Dentistry Cairo Egypt

## Abstract

The spectrum of socio‐economic backgrounds can lead to an unpredictable range of social interactions between patients and prospective dentists. Tolerance is essential for patient relationships and conflict resolution, making it a topic of significant scientific and practical importance. This study aimed to explore the tolerance levels of dental students at King Abdulaziz University (KAU) towards their patients in relation to the students' associated circumstances.

A self‐administered questionnaire was used to assess the tolerance level of dental interns and senior dental students of KAU towards their patients. The Likert scale was used in the questionnaire with bi‐directional questions with points allocated. The questionnaire assessed demographic data and lifestyle patterns of the participant as well as the participant's tolerance towards various clinical scenarios involving patients of different nationalities and behaviours.

In this study, 193 participants out of 254 completed the questionnaire, for a response rate of 75.98%. The dental interns reported more tolerance than 6th‐year dental students, and students with a grade point average score of ‘B' were found to be more tolerant than those with other scores. Male and female students were more tolerant of different parameters. Diet and sleep could not be directly correlated to tolerance. Married students and students living with family exhibited higher tolerance than single students and those living alone.

This study established a variety of factors that can influence tolerance levels. It would be informative to conduct future investigations with a broader range of patients and analyse the relationship between tolerance and other emotional parameters.

## Introduction

The fast‐paced, demanding environment of dental school can create an emotional imbalance in dental students, resulting in various adverse physical and mental symptoms [1]. Common sources of stress can include the rigorous academic workload, frequent scholastic and clinical examinations, lack of free/leisure time, requirements to complete multiple physically demanding procedures, time constraints, inexperience, lack of confidence and conflicts that can occur with patients, colleagues and faculty [1, 2]. These high levels of stress over a long period of time can lead to ‘burnout’, a state of complete mental, emotional and physical exhaustion that can result in depersonalisation, reduced personal accomplishment, diminished work efficiency, absenteeism and the related physical and psychological effects of stress [3]. It was reported that intense interactions between the dentist and the patient could generate ‘burnout’ [4].

The Member States of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation in 1995 presented Articles 1.1 and 1.2 in which ‘tolerance’ was defined as ‘respect, acceptance and appreciation of the rich diversity of our world's cultures, our forms of expression, and ways of being human… [it] is an active attitude prompted by recognition of the universal human rights and fundamental freedoms of others’ [5]. Tolerance refers to the ability of an individual to accept and respect differences in opinions, backgrounds and cultures [6]. In the context of dental education, tolerance also refers to a student's capacity to accept and manage the stresses and strains of his or her relationships with patients, colleagues and faculty. Tolerance is a crucial component for dental students to develop the necessary skills to navigate the challenges of their education and future careers. By understanding the relationship between tolerance and stress, further solutions can be implemented to manage the stress successfully, address conflicts and promote effective communication. The desired outcome would be to provide the means for students to adapt to the difficult situations, develop stronger interpersonal skills, improve patient care and enhance their physical and mental well‐being as well as their personal growth [7].

Similarly, tolerance and emotional integrity are closely interlinked, as they both involve genuine and authentic self‐reflection and interaction with others, and the acceptance of different perspectives and emotions. Emotional integrity can be defined as consistently being honest with oneself and others in thoughts, feelings and actions. It refers to the ability to recognise, express, and work with one's emotions in a healthy and constructive way [8]. Embodying emotional integrity leads to the genuine respect and acceptance of others' emotions and perspectives, a focal cornerstone of tolerance. Trust and respect fostered through emotional integrity create a foundation where tolerance can thrive. As these two are mutually reinforcing, it is significant to note that the resultant synergy not only enhances personal relationships but also contributes to a more inclusive and accepting society [9].

Most studies evaluate stress levels among dental students by interrelating them to factors such as age, gender, marital status, academic year and curriculum requirements [10]. Polychronopoulou and Divaris conducted a study on dental students and found that female students are 40% more stressed than male students, which was similarly reported by other researchers [11]. Married subjects perceived more stress than single subjects with regard to patient treatment, performance pressure and social stressors [12]. The studies documented the sources of the stress, perceived stress or coping modalities in the dental environment. Some of the highest‐ranking stressors were the patients and the related situations regarding their demands, behaviours, and pressures to meet expectations [10].

Dental treatment is a collaborative effort between the dentist and the patient. Previous dental experiences, discrepancies in expectations, and language barriers can create miscommunication and frustration in the treatment process [13]. The diversity in the patient pool comes with socio‐economic and cultural variations that can propagate these issues and may disorient dental students still learning to navigate the other facets of their education. The rapidly evolving landscape of intermingling diversities invokes the question: how tolerant are dental students towards their patients?

King Abdulaziz University Dental Hospital receives a diverse variety of patients [14]. It resides in Jeddah, a coastal city in Saudi Arabia, where a little over 40% of the population are non‐Saudis according to the United Nations Habitat City‐Prospect‐Index report from 2019 [15]. The dental students are primarily Saudi Arabian, although not necessarily original Jeddah residents. The spectrum of socio‐economic backgrounds, cultural influence, and religious impact leads to an unpredictable and wide range of social interactions between the patients and dentists‐to‐be [16, 17]. To the best of our knowledge, no article has been found that relates dental students' stressors to the level of tolerance among dental students towards their patients. This study aimed to explore these relationships and the associated circumstances of King Abdulaziz University (KAU) dental students and interns to better understand the factors that affect their tolerance capacity.

## Materials and Methods

An ethical approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee at KAU (#076‐09‐17). The study was conducted with undergraduate senior dental students and dental interns at KAU in the academic year 2022–2023.

A self‐administered questionnaire was created by the authors to assess the tolerance level of dental interns and senior dental students towards their patients based on the most common stressors that the subjects could face. The questionnaire consisted of five sections with a total of 33 questions. They were categorised as A, Demographic; B, Lifestyle; C, Tolerance to nationality, ethnicity and behaviour; D, Tolerance towards clinical situations and E, Emotional integrity. The tolerance level in section ‘C' contained questions involving the participants' tolerance towards patients’ nationalities, ethnicity and behaviour (with the categories of behaviour being philosophical, exacting, complaining or indifferent) [18]. Section ‘D’ contained questions involving clinical situations (with the categories of situations being difficult procedures, long procedures, late patients, barriers to care such as language and transportation, patients with disabilities, uncooperative and unmotivated patients, patients with uncontrolled and controlled medical conditions, working under time pressure, abrupt changes in treatment plans, patients moving mid‐treatment, and unsatisfied patients) Section ‘E’ contained questions pertaining to the emotional response of the subject.

The Likert scale was used in the questionnaire with bi‐directional types of questions. Thirty‐three criteria were measured on a 5‐point scale with a minimum score of 33 and a maximum score of 165. For all the categories like ‘patient behaviour’, ‘clinical situations’ and ‘emotional integrity’, a score > 73% denoted a high tolerance, which meant that the subject was not hindered or stressed by the factor. A score in the range of 46%–72.9% represented a medium tolerance, and a score in the range of 18%–45.9% signified a low tolerance, which meant that the subject found the factor to be impeding or stressful.

The sample size was calculated to be within 5 percentage points (with 95% certainty). To evaluate whether the questions effectively captured the tolerance level, the validity of the questionnaire was checked by experts in Health Professions Education among the faculty with credentials in dental education and experience in education‐focused research. Afterwards, a pilot study among dental academic staff and dental students was conducted and checked for internal consistency and reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.951).

The questionnaire was distributed by the research team members to all registered dental interns (after the 6th year, students are required to take a 1‐year clinical internship at several governmental dental facilities) and to the senior year students (6th‐year dental students; the KAU dental program spans 6 years) during the academic year 2022–2023 (n = 254). 32% of 6th‐year students dropped out as they did not want to participate. The remaining participants were 193–125 dental interns and 67 senior year students. Consent was implied by agreeing to complete the questionnaire.

The data obtained by the questionnaire were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), Version 21 (IBM Inc., Armonk, NY, USA). Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests were conducted to test for normality of the data. Categorical variables were presented as numbers and percentages and were compared using the chi‐squared test and the Monte Carlo test. Continuous variables were normally distributed, presented as mean and standard deviation (SD), and were compared using an independent t‐test and a one‐way ANOVA test. All tests were two‐tailed, and a p‐value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

In this study, 193 participants out of 254 completed the questionnaire, for a response rate of 75.98%. Results demonstrated varying levels of tolerance that were significantly correlated with gender (p < 0.05). Moreover, the level of tolerance for various emotional integrities was significantly correlated with gender (p = 0.008) (Figure 1). There was a statistically significant association between tolerance levels in correlation with gender (p = 0.001); however, there was no statistically significant correlation between gender and the degree of tolerance for patients' behaviour (p = 0.058) or various clinical conditions (p = 0.39) (Figure 2).

*FIGURE 1: Association between overall tolerance level with gender. A statistically significant association was found between overall tolerance levels in relation to gender. The chi‐squared test was applied at a 95% confidence interval (p = 0.001).*

*FIGURE 2: A representation of the significant association between different situations with gender regarding tolerance level (p < 0.05).*

When assessing tolerance with marital status, a statistically significant association was found (p = 0.004) (Figure 3). However, there was no correlation between the participants' marital status and level of tolerance with regard to the patients' nationality and ethnicity (p = 0.37), behaviour (p = 0.75) and various clinical scenarios (p = 0.78). Similarly, assessing tolerance with place of living also demonstrated a significant association (p = 0.04) (Figure 4). ## Discussion

The stress experienced by dental students is diverse. Dental environmental stressors represent external components, while the physiological and biochemical reactions from the student's body in response to the perceived stress represent internal components. The interaction between the external and internal components generates coping mechanisms [19]. The primary factors motivating dentists to retire early were discovered to be musculoskeletal problems, burnout and stress‐related ailments [20].

Lazarus and Folkman hypothesised that, rather than the individual demands themselves, how students manage the demands of education as a whole may be the main factor influencing their psychological suffering [21]. Several studies carried out at dentistry schools all over the world have thoroughly delved into the main aspects of stress experienced uniquely by the dental student [2]. Even though the majority of these studies had a cross‐sectional design, they have demonstrated a considerable rise in stress among dentistry students in connection with several variables [22].

Tolerance is necessary in maintaining peaceful coexistence and resolving conflict, which makes it a topic of great scientific and practical magnitude. The intrinsic issues surrounding tolerance remain empirical puzzles, and the many branching facets of tolerance are still being explored [23]. For dentists, tolerance is a double‐ended exchange in the dentist–patient relationship. The patient endures the procedures, despite their discomfort, which can manifest as vasovagal syncope, crying, rage or refusal of treatment [24]. The dentist ‘tolerates’ the issues that arise from patient care, which are typically difficult treatments, combative or aggressive patients, fearful or anxious patients, patient non‐compliance during treatment and other work‐associated disruptions to operating [25].

This was the first study that focused on the tolerance level of KAU dental interns and senior dental students towards their patients. The subjects of the study were questioned on their capacity to tolerate patient‐related factors, with a low tolerance indicating that the subject found the factor to be hinderingly stressful. Overall, the present study found a high tolerance level among the subjects, suggesting that the patient‐related factors did not affect the students' work capacity. This might be related to the strict rules and regulations in the work environment, the diverse population of Jeddah, and the students' inherent values and ethics. However, a closer examination of the individual factors contributing to that tolerance result reveals a more comprehensive analysis of the elements influencing the dental students.

The KAU dentistry program spans 6 years, followed by a mandatory 1‐year clinical internship. Students first enter the clinics and begin treating patients during their 4th year, with the number of clinical requirements and difficulty of cases increasing each year [26]. Once 6th‐year students finish their clinical and academic requirements at the end of the year, they graduate into interns, who are given a rotating schedule of hospitals and institutions that they must work at. The clinical requirements are fewer in the internship year as the interns migrate between different clinical settings and can even choose to work at specific departments with specialties that interest them. Given these circumstances, interns have more experience and confidence and fewer time constraints than students [27]. That is probably why the results reflected that—the interns demonstrated more tolerant behaviour than 6th‐year students.

In this study, the age range of the dental students at KAU was between 18 and 28 years, with most students being single (~85%). A majority reported living with their family (~83%), as this is a cultural norm in Saudi Arabia, and people will typically live at home with their parents until marriage [28]. Participants living with family demonstrated significantly higher tolerance levels than those living with a roommate or alone. The varying conditions of the intricate structure of family relationships make defining the nature of the factor unpredictable. Family can be a support system for some, and a source of stress for others, especially among parents with demanding expectations [29]. Some studies report that those living alone have more positive mental health, while other studies emphasise that living alone worsens depression and can exacerbate chronic health conditions [29, 30, 31]. Nevertheless, the social interactions between family members, whether a source of support or stress, can teach mediation, adaptability and communication [32].

In a similar regard, the participants who were married with children were found to be the most tolerant when compared to childless married or single participants. This is probably due to the adaptive nature parents adopt with raising children, as well as the conflict‐resolution mindset that is gradually learnt by maintaining social, financial and family responsibilities as a student, parent and spouse [1]. There was no significant association between the students' and interns' marital status and their level of tolerance towards various clinical scenarios and patients of different ethnicities and nationalities. This indicates that the students'/interns' marital status held no influence on their conduct or emotional integrity in their relationships with their patients.

In terms of gender, males were found to be more tolerant of ‘demanding patients’ and ‘working under pressure', whereas females were more tolerant of ‘patients’ nationalities and ethnicities', ‘patients' behaviour’, ‘flexibility in treatment’ and ‘appointment adjustment’. There was no statistically significant relationship between gender and tolerance with regard to various clinical scenarios. Females were overall found to be more tolerant than males. It's important to note that tolerance is not directly proportional to stress. While the degree of stress experienced between the genders could be different, the degree of tolerance speaks to the adaptability of the individual. The patriarchal nature of Saudi Arabian society is deeply rooted in its history, culture and religious interpretations, and as a result, females tend to comply and adapt more often than males do, as seen in studies with similar patriarchal societies [33, 34]. Research in psychology and sociology supports the idea that females are often socialised to be more cooperative, as they are encouraged to develop relational skills and social harmony, in part as a strategy to manage and survive within patriarchal constraints [35]. The levels of stress among female dental students have previously been attributed to the societal construct of masculinity, according to which men exhibit stress less openly but are consequently more susceptible to health concerns [19].

Academic performance is essential for achieving academic success, as it enhances students' competitiveness in the job market and serves as a significant indicator of their future occupational success, although some researchers argue otherwise [36]. KAU operates on a grade point average out of 5. ‘B‐students’ were found to be more tolerant than the other groups. This could be due to the balance between optimum effort and low demand. ‘A‐students’ who tend to demonstrate stricter perfectionism could have been less inclined to exhibit relaxed attitudes with their patients [2]. Ihm et al. conducted a study on what cognitive and non‐cognitive factors were responsible for predicting the academic performance of dental students. They found that students' interpersonal skills were negatively related to their academic performance [37]. Weil and Inglehart highlighted a correlation between general dentists' reported use of appropriate behaviour management strategies for patients with special needs and the quality of their educational experiences [38]. Jahan et al. stated that patient dissatisfaction in dental practices can frequently stem from the dentist's inadequate communication skills, despite their strong academic knowledge and technical expertise, and that emotional intelligence and empathy are necessary for professional competence [39]. These studies emphasise the importance of developing effective communication, interpersonal and empathetic skills to prepare students for successful careers in dentistry.

Sleep influences physical, social and mental health, and lack of sufficient sleep is known to cause many physical and mental strains such as exhaustion, irritability, lowered levels of attention, elevated levels of anxiety, impaired cognitive performance and may compromise memory and decision‐making [40]. In this study, subjects with less than four hours of sleep were less tolerant, while higher amounts of sleep were associated with greater tolerance. However, due to the multifaceted nature of sleep, it is difficult to correlate this factor to the subject's tolerance, as the association could be spurious. Nevertheless, lack of sleep is a persistent issue for dental students that can cause long‐term harm to academic and clinical performance, social standing and conduct and may worsen feelings of burnout [40, 41]. Though it is challenging to implement a protocol to help dental students in this regard, tailored interventions can be a helpful consideration when dental students feel overwhelmed and request support.

Diet also affects physical and mental health, with poor nutrition leading to acute mood alterations, systemic inflammation, and negative effects stemming from the bidirectional relationship between the gut microbiome and brain function [42]. Poor diets are often found among college students due to their stressful lifestyles and busy schedules [43]. Furthermore, adults in Saudi Arabia also typically demonstrate poor nutrition behaviour and dietary habits [44, 45]. The results in this study reported that those with a healthy diet exhibited high tolerance, with a decrease in tolerance in mixed diets and significantly reduced tolerance in diets consisting only of junk food. Although this indicates that diet can relatively affect an individual's behaviour, it cannot be directly correlated to tolerance levels, as with ‘hours of sleep’, the result could have been affected by other confounders. Previous studies have reported strong associations between poor diet quality and various negative mental effects; however, more comprehensive investigations need to be conducted to fully affirm these effects [46].

The revised House classification of patients is taught to students as part of their curriculum. This classification refers to profiling the behaviour of a patient according to clinical impressions. In this study, the categories used were philosophical, exacting, complaining (instead of hysterical) and indifferent. Philosophical refers to an engaging and trusting patient, exacting refers to a challenging and untrusting patient, complaining refers to a reluctant and resisting patient, and indifferent refers to a minimally engaged and uninterested patient [18]. The management and care of all these patients require years of training and experience. Despite the categorization, no one ‘type' of behaviour can be managed in a singular manner—rather, each case is unique and must be approached through the individuality of the patient. This classification serves to familiarise students with the behaviour of patients they can expect to meet and also allows them to form expectations when delivering treatment. The senior dental students and interns reported a high tolerance to the different behaviours of their patients. Evaluating the tolerance of 5th‐ and 4th‐year students may yield more variable results.

Dental schools should promote and present resources and support systems to aid students in managing their stress levels. This can include therapy and counselling services, peer‐support groups, campaigns to foster healthy lifestyle habits and self‐care practice encouragement [19]. In particular, implementing conflict‐resolution strategies can be a great help in assisting students in navigating their struggles and improving their tolerance. Disputes between the dental provider and the patient are inevitable in the healthcare environment, and so it is crucial to address conflicts promptly and effectively. Conflict resolution training programs, open dialogues and safe spaces for students to express concerns allow for personal growth and can, in turn, help students build resilience, empathy and tolerance towards their patients [17, 47].

Additionally, dental schools should ensure faculty and staff are trained to recognise the signs of stress and intolerance and provide appropriate support and interventions. Dental schools should provide professional development opportunities for faculty to augment their communication capacity, mentorship skills and emotional competency. By fostering an environment of support, dental schools can allow students to feel valued, less isolated, and improve their overall well‐being. This will also improve their patient relationships, conduct, and potential for success [48].

### Limitations and Future Perspectives

The limitation of the study lies in the difficulty of capturing the wide array of complex behaviours, emotions and motivations that an individual undergoes with regard to tolerance. The uniqueness of the study stems from recognising the societal differences that exist in Saudi Arabia. The cultural norm leans towards conservatism, and the scale of tolerance that exists for the typical Saudi Arabian dental student operates on a different spectrum than what would exist for dental students raised in other societies. Establishing protocols to educate students and address their concerns and tolerance levels could allow for improved behaviour, which can be assessed in a future study. Moreover, further exploration into the psycho‐social relationships between the dental student and patient may aid in improving trust, communication and rapport.

## Conclusion

Our study revealed that KAU dental students demonstrated an overall high tolerance level towards their patients. When assessing individual parameters, academic level, gender, marital status and place of living have an influence on tolerance level. Hence, it is imperative to educate students in behavioural sciences and develop strategies to improve their tolerance level by integrating communication skills and professionalism into the dental curriculum.

Purpose: Nanoparticles and natural products have gained attention for their beneficial properties, but limited studies exist on the coadministration of these two therapeutic agents. In this study, both magnesium oxide nanoparticles (MgO NPs) and royal jelly (RJ) were evaluated for their protective potential against parotid gland damage in induced diabetic rats through the investigation of their antidiabetic, antioxidative, and anti-inflammatory effects. Material and Methods: 64 male rats were divided into 8 groups: control group, MgO NPs treated group (300mg/kg/day), RJ treated group (100mg/kg/day), streptozotocin-induced diabetic group, diabetic group and concomitant MgO NPs, diabetic group and concomitant RJ, diabetic group and co-administration of both MgO NPs and RJ, and diabetic group and concomitant metformin (100mg/kg/day). After 8 weeks, the rats of all groups were anaesthetized, and blood was drawn to estimate different diabetic parameters. Saliva was collected to determine the salivary parameters. The parotid glands were excised and cut into pieces, where half was frozen for further biochemical investigations (oxidative stress and inflammatory markers) and the other assessed for histological and immunohistochemical changes. Introduction Diabetes mellitus (DM) is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia, resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. This persistent elevation in blood glucose leads to a range of metabolic disturbances in carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism. Insulin-dependent tissues experience a reduction in glucose uptake, which, in turn, stimulates increased glucose production by the liver and the breakdown of glycogen. Additionally, lipid metabolism is disrupted, leading to higher levels of free fatty acids and triglycerides, thereby exacerbating insulin resistance and lipotoxicity. These metabolic disorders collectively lead to both acute and chronic complications, which can include vascular damage, oxidative stress, and inflammation.1,2

Many components of the body are affected by DM, and the oral cavity is no exception. The major oral manifestations can present as xerostomia (dry mouth), soft tissue inflammation, periodontal disease, dental caries, oral candidiasis, burning mouth, altered taste, heightened infection susceptibility, and impaired wound healing.3 The literature has recently demonstrated that DM modifies the tissue structure and mechanism of saliva secretion, thereby precipitating xerostomia.4

Many diabetic patients experience hypofunction of the salivary glands, which can worsen and result in hyposalivation.5

Parotid gland alteration is commonly observed in diabetic individuals. Approximately 80% of diabetic patients exhibit sialadenosis, a non-inflammatory and asymptomatic enlargement of the parotid glands. Ultrasonographic studies further support these findings, revealing increased glandular volume in diabetic individuals compared to healthy controls, with such changes closely associated with the duration of diabetes and the level of glycemic control.6,7

Beyond the well-documented impact on the parotid glands, DM also significantly impairs the function and structure of the submandibular, sublingual, and minor salivary glands.8 Collectively, these alterations contribute to the pathogen­ esis of xerostomia and other oral health issues frequently observed in diabetic individuals.4,9,10

The pathogenesis of DM-related salivary gland hypofunction occurs as a result of the persistent hyperglycemia generating oxidative and cellular damage, which in turn hinders the structure of the tissues.3 Chronic oxidative stress induces the excessive production of reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating the complications associated with DM.11 Reports have mentioned that DM-associated neuropathy, microvascular abnormalities, endothelial dysfunction, and hindered microcirculation could lead to degenerative changes in salivary glands.12

Currently, the most commonly used drug for the treatment of DM is metformin, with other available treatments such as sulfonylureas, thiazolidinedione, α-glucosidase inhibitors, repaglinide, and insulin therapies. However, while these treatments can reverse hyperglycemia temporarily, they possess numerous side effects in the form of hyponatremia (abnormally low sodium in the blood), obstructive jaundice, nausea, headaches, vomiting, and weight gain. Long-term insulin administration from an external source can gradually diminish insulin formation and secretion in β-cells.13 The suggested medical treatments for diabetes-associated hyposalivation and xerostomia include artificial saliva spray, chemical reagents such as malic acid and locarpine, and systemic sialagogues. Nonetheless, these provide only a temporary alleviation of the salivary flow rate and can trigger adverse effects like excessive sweating, tremors,

Additionally, implementing natural compounds and supplements into therapeutic agents has become progres­ sively prevalent. Discussion The pathogenesis of parotid gland damage in DM is multifactorial, primarily driven by chronic hyperglycemia, which induces metabolic disturbances that impair glandular function. Increased glucose levels lead to the creation of advanced glycation end-products, which interfere with normal cellular functions and cause tissue damage. Moreover, DM is marked by increased oxidative stress arising from an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the body’s antioxidant defenses, resulting in damage to the structure and function of salivary glands. Microangiopathy further compromises blood supply to these glands, resulting in hypoxia and nutrient deficiencies that contribute to atrophy and reduced secretory capacity. Moreover, diabetic neuropathy can impair autonomic control of salivary secretion, exacer­ bating xerostomia and worsening oral health outcomes.43–45

Given the individual therapeutic approaches of MgO NPs and RJ, this study was devised as a novel approach to utilize the benefits of both to manage parotid gland dysfunction that occurs as a complication of DM, which can considerably worsen the patient’s quality of life and increase the possibility of periodontitis and other oral infections.

The quality and yield of the MgO NPs were confirmed through a qualitative assessment using XRD, FTIR, and ZP. These analytical techniques are suitable and effective in providing information on the composition and interactions of nanomaterials; however, some previous investigations have reported that the results depend on various factors such as particle size, distribution, shape, aggregation, and surface charge of the tested nanoparticles.46 The MgO NPs’ nature was highly crystalline and exhibited physical stability when suspended in water. Our findings agreed with previously published works that reported similar results.38,47

Metformin (dimethyl biguanide) was used in this study as a standard oral antidiabetic drug, as it is commonly prescribed to lower blood glucose levels in patients with non-insulin-dependent DM.48 Investigations have demonstrated its efficacy in blood sugar control with low risk of hypoglycemia, although common side-effects can include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and vitamin B12 deficiency.49,50 Throughout the various investigations in our study, our results expressed that the administration of both MgO NPs and RJ to diabetic rats was comparable or superior in promoting good results of the diabetic and oxidative stress parameters in comparison to metformin.

The streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats showed a notable rise in blood glucose levels and a reduction in SI levels, together with an increase of HOMA-IR; these findings were consistent with former studies which stated that hyperglycemia can be considered a direct reflex to the marked hypo-insulinemia caused by the selective destructive cytotoxic effect of streptozotocin on the β-cells of the pancreas.51,52

The administration of both MgO NPs and RJ to the diabetic rats notably improved these parameters, affirming their antidiabetic effect. In this regard, some recent studies have validated the efficacy of MgO NPs as antidiabetics, where they play a role in improving glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity in diabetic rats.53–55 Through the regulation of blood sugar levels, MgO NPs can reduce the severity of DM-related complications.38 MgO NPs have been found to improve insulin sensitivity in animal and cell levels, which in turn induces the receptivity of the body’s cells to insulin and therefore facilitates the reduction of blood glucose and lowers the risk of developing Type 2 DM.56,57 These effects may be due to the physicochemical characteristics inherent to nanoparticles, allowing for increased uptake.16 Moreover, the small size allows for close interaction with biological tissue.17

Additionally, it was reported that magnesium is a necessary cofactor for enzymes shared in carbohydrate metabolism, particularly in the phosphorylation of tyrosine-kinase of the insulin receptor, along with all other protein kinases involved in insulin signaling.21,57,58 This is in accordance with previous studies, which reported that DM is associated with intracellular and extracellular magnesium depletion, and magnesium augmentation positively influences insulin receptor activity and reduces insulin resistance in a rat model.59,60

Likewise, administration of RJ presented a significant decrease in the elevated glucose level and a significant increase in insulin concentration. Moreover, studies have illustrated that supplying RJ to diabetic rats lead to a significant alleviation of glucose, insulin, and insulin resistance.61,62 Ghanbari et al demonstrated that diabetic rats fed 100mg/kg of RJ for eight weeks had decreased fasting blood glucose and increased serum insulin levels.63 Furthermore, RJ was found to regulate and reduce blood sugar levels through activity analogous to insulin, thereby improving insulin resistance in the rats.32 Additionally, Mousavi et al conducted a randomized controlled trial on 46 diabetic patients

The level of MDA, a marker of oxidative stress, was significantly higher in the parotid tissue of the diabetic group, together with a marked reduction in the levels of antioxidant enzymes SOD, GPx, and CAT, suggesting oxidative damage in this gland. Some studies stated that the increased oxidative stress found with DM can lead to tissue damage of the parotid gland.65,66 The parotid gland is particularly susceptible to antioxidant imbalances and oxidative damage due to its predominantly aerobic metabolism and its inherent defense mechanisms against reactive oxygen species.4,67

Studies have previously demonstrated that hyperglycemia significantly impacts the parotid gland, leading to increased lipid peroxidation, elevated MDA levels, and a reduction in antioxidant enzyme activity.4,68 Additionally, it was stated that in DM, the antioxidant enzymes are significantly reduced in many tissues, resulting in sustained reactive oxygen species formation, thereby heightening oxidative stress and leading to nuclear apoptosis and cellular degeneration in both the parotid and submandibular glands.69,70 Therefore, it can be concluded that the use of antioxidants is beneficial as an additional treatment for DM.71,72

In this regard, the concurrent administration of both MgO NPs and RJ to the diabetic rats presented defensive characteristics through the significant reduction in MDA levels and significant elevation in catalase activity and GPx. One key mechanism through which MgO NPs exert their protective effects is by acting as antioxidants.38,53 MgO NPs can scavenge free radicals and reduce oxidative stress, thus aiding in the preservation of the structural and functional integrity of the parotid gland in diabetic conditions.18 Moreover, MgO NPs may modulate the inflammatory responses, which are often worsened in DM.73 By reducing inflammation, these nanoparticles can aid in protecting the parotid gland against DM-induced damage. A study by Moeini-Nodeh et al illustrated MgO NPs’ capacity to prompt anti-oxidative, anti-diabetic, and anti-apoptotic functions in the pancreatic islet.74

Furthermore, a growing body of evidence suggests that RJ has the ability to diminish oxidative stress through its role as a free-radical scavenger, maintain an adequate antioxidant status, and protect against toxicity induced by reactive oxygen species.25,75 Maleki et al conducted a systematic review on the metabolic effects of RJ in diabetic patients and stated that RJ intake could improve glycemic status, HOMA-IR, lipid profiles, and oxidative stress.23 It has also been reported to enhance levels and activity of the antioxidant enzymes CAT and SOD.20,76,77

In this study, the diabetic rats had a marked decrease in salivary secretion parameters (salivary flow rate, sAA, and total protein content) compared to the control values. These findings coincided with previous human studies, which stated that most diabetic patients experience hypofunction of salivary glands, and further exacerbation can result in hyposaliva­ tion or xerostomia.5,78,79 Additionally, our results were in accordance with animal studies, which reported the deteriora­ tion of these salivary parameters resulting in the decline of secretory dysfunction in salivary glands, especially in the parotid gland.80,81

Moreover, DM can lead to diabetic autonomic neuropathy, a complication that disrupts autonomic control of salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands. Since salivary secretion depends on a balance between parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous inputs, autonomic dysfunction in diabetes can impair salivary flow and composition. This may manifest as xerostomia and increased susceptibility to oral infections. Structural changes in the parotid glands, such as acinar atrophy and reduced expression of key proteins like aquaporin-5, further contribute to glandular dysfunction.82

The conditions of DM result in the alteration of salivary gland tissue structure and the mechanism of saliva secretion.4,83 In the present study, the histopathology of the parotid gland of the diabetic rats displayed multiple lesions, including disorganization and atrophic changes in the serous acini, vacuolization and degeneration of both acinar and ductal cells, inflammatory cell infiltration, and accumulation of increased collagen fibers. These results were consistent with several previous studies conducted in rats in which DM induces morphological alterations in salivary glands, with changes seen in the density of secretory granules health.80,84,85

The results also exhibited that many serous acini of the parotid gland of diabetic rats showed atrophic changes with cytoplasmic vacuolization and apoptotic nuclei of the acinar cells. Chen et al confirmed this, noting significant acinar cell deformation and atrophy, along with a reduction in secretory granules and vacuolation among the diabetic rats.4 Such findings were explained by the accumulation of degenerative substances and fatty degeneration in the cytoplasm, as well as the DM-induced oxidative stress in the parotid glands and the associated degenerative changes.69,85 Consistent with

The administration of both MgO NPs and RJ to the diabetic rats established a beneficial role in improving the salivary secretion parameters towards the normal values. A recent study has shown that 12 weeks of RJ tablets (800 mg daily) were effective for patients who suffered from subjective dry mouth sensation with normal saliva function.87 While many studies promote the benefits of oral consumption of magnesium, limited studies exist on the oral consumption of MgO NPs in humans, with most studies conducted in animals and focused on addressing cytotoxicity concerns.22,88,89 In consensus, most concluded that low doses of MgO NPs provided benefits with no cytotoxicity, while higher doses could produce significant tissue damage.74,90–92 Further toxicological profiling and biomedical investigations are imperative in determining safe exposure levels to utilize the multi-faceted benefits of MgO NPs.

In the present study, a significant increase in collagen deposition and dilated, congested blood vessels around the ducts was observed in the DM group. These findings coincide with what was detected by El Shahawy and El Deeb, who similarly found thick networks of collagen fiber bundles surrounding the blood vessels of the submandibular salivary gland in diabetic rats.93 This could be attributed to the hyperglycemia triggering disordered remodeling activity of fibroblasts along with the inflammatory process associated with DM.69,94

A marked improvement occurred in these histopathological alterations in the parotid gland of diabetic rats upon concurrent administration of MgO NPs and RJ. These results agreed with some recent studies that reported that MgO NPs possess antioxidant properties, which are essential for combating oxidative stress.22,95 Moreover, it was reported that RJ resulted in a decrease of oxidative stress indicators and an increase in antioxidant enzyme levels.25,77

The immunohistochemical study of α-SMA expression, which is an important immunohistochemical marker for myoepithelial cells, showed a marked reduction in the parotid gland of the diabetic group as compared to the control group. It was reported that in the salivary glands, myoepithelial cells are stellate cells generally in the form of arcs surrounding the acini and appear along the long axes of the ducts. Their main function is to facilitate the expulsion of secretion from the acini.96 This was similarly reported in diabetic mice by Nashida et al.97 However, in another study by Morsy et al, the diabetic parotid glands showed a notably greater expression of α-SMA immunoreaction compared to the control group, suggesting a disproportionate proliferation or hypertrophy of myoepithelial cells.86

The immunohistochemical study of TP53 displayed a higher expression in the parotid gland of diabetic rats compared to the control. TP53 is known to regulate cell survival and death, and animal studies have shown that it also responds to metabolic changes and affects metabolic pathways.98 Several studies have established that chronic hyperglycemia causes cellular damage through oxidative injury to lipids, proteins, and DNA, which activates TP53. Subsequently, this activation controls the expression of apoptotic, pro-inflammatory, and metabolic genes.99,100 The administration of both MgO NPs and RJ to the diabetic rats showed mild p53 immuno-expression in the parotid gland, indicating stimulation of the antioxidant pathway. This illustrates that histological improvement could be a response to low levels of oxidative stress as a result of their antioxidant effect that stimulates p53.101

Several challenges were faced during this study. While combining STZ and a high carbohydrate diet is often used to mimic diabetes, these models may not accurately reproduce the complexities of β-cell dysfunction seen in humans. Furthermore, the effect of long-term complications could not be assessed within the eight-week time frame of the study. Alternative parameters and DM-associated complications should also be assessed.

Conclusion The present study demonstrated that both MgO NPs and RJ exhibit promising effects in the defense against parotid gland damage in diabetic rats, which was more profound when these two agents were used together, as their synergetic actions were found to have significant hypoglycemic, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, further clinical trials are needed to cement the validity of the dual administration of MgO NPs and RJ to diabetic patients.

# Mechanical Behaviour of Novel Nanohybrid Resin Composite Using Two Light Cure Systems

**Authors:** Ghada H. Naguib; Jumana Mazhar; Abeer Alnowaiser; Abdulghani Mira; Hisham Mously; Rabab Aljawi; Samar H. Abuzinadah; Mohamed T. Hamed

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Restorative Dentistry, Faculty of Dentistry, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia | bKing Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia | cDepartment of Pediatric Dentistry, Faculty of Dentistry, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia | dDepartment of Oral and Maxillofacial Prosthodontics, Faculty of Dentistry, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia

## Abstract

Zein-incorporated magnesium oxide nanoparticles (zMgO NPs) were found to be effective against the bacteria S. mutans, S. aureus, E. faecalis and C. albicans, and can impart this antimicrobial effect on the resin composite it is integrated with. However, the effect of different light curing systems on the mechanical properties of this novel biomaterial has yet to be investigated. The objective of this study was to assess the effect of light-emitting diode (LED) and quarts-tungsten halogen (QTH) light curing systems on the compressive strength, flexural strength, and microhardness of bulk-fill resin composite modified with zMgO NPs.

A Teflon mold was used to fabricate 180 bulk-fill composite samples with concentrations of zMgO NPs at 0%, 0.3% and 0.5% (n = 60). Samples of each group were allocated to light curing by LED or QTH, after which 10 samples of each group were allotted to a mechanical test. Characterization of the specimens was performed by X-ray diffraction, field emission scanning electron microscopy and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. Two-way ANOVA and Tukey's post-hoc test was conducted at P = .05 to determine significance.

The characterization revealed a uniform distribution of nanoparticles in the matrix and the formation of a new hybrid composite that maintained its properties. The compressive strength of the 0.3% zMgO composite for the QTH group significantly increased, while the remaining groups underwent no significant change. There was no significant difference among the groups for the flexural strength and microhardness tests.

The modified composites’ compressive strength, flexural strength, and microhardness improved or remained consistent. Long-term clinical studies can further substantiate the enhanced resin composite.

The modified composite will exhibit similar or improved mechanical properties whether an LED or QTH light cure device is used. The addition of an antimicrobial effect to bulk-fill resin composite will aid in the prevention of secondary caries.

## Introduction

As secondary caries still exists as the most common cause of failure in resin composite restorations, it stands to reason that improvements to resin composite needs to be made to counter this issue.1 Bulk-fill composite (BFC) has been introduced for use over conventional composite as it as faster alternative with similar mechanical properties. It is placed in increments of 4-5 mm (depending on the brand) rather than increments of 2 mm, which is the standard recommendation for conventional composite.2 Some studies have reported that the BFC experiences similar or less polymerization shrinkage, mechanical wear and marginal gaps when compared to conventional composite.3,4 However, not enough long-term clinical studies on BFC exist to validate the outcome over a long period of time.

The integration of inorganic particles under 100 nm in diameter with resin composites was another potential explored in the improvement of the dental material. The miniscule dimension of the nanoparticles and their capacity to occupy a large surface area relative to their small volume enables interaction with the resin matrix on a superior scale.5 Furthermore, the usage of particular nanoparticles has been reported to exhibit antimicrobial behaviour, which is adopted by the modified resin composite.[5], [6], [7] This alteration would be crucial in resisting bacterial contamination and secondary caries. However, several barriers must be bypassed to fully improve the modified composite.

Firstly, the surface atoms of nanoparticles contain surface tension, which is the extra energy that is generated as a result of the unsatisfied bonding of those surface atoms due to the lack of neighbours to bind to. The outcome is that the nanoparticles tend to agglomerate, which would transform them to a larger-sized filler, thereby losing the unique properties that exist at the nano-scale.8,9 Secondly, the documentation on the influence of the integration of nanoparticles on the mechanical properties of the modified resin composite is still limited. While studies have shown that the anti-bacterial effect exists, this property cannot be utilized if it compromises the mechanical properties, and by extension the longevity, of the dental material.5,7

Magnesium oxide nanoparticles have exceptional biocompatibility, bactericidal properties, and capacity for bone repair, but had been overlooked due to the agglomeration issue.[10], [11], [12] Recently, it was discovered that zein, a natural corn polymer commonly used in the pharmaceutical industry, was capable of acting as a silane coupling agent and stabilizing the nanoparticles, enabling them to maintain their nano-characteristics.13 Furthermore, this addition did not affect the magnesium oxide nanoparticles antibacterial effect, as the zMgO NPs were found to be highly effective against the four bacteria S. mutans, S. aureus, E. faecalis, and C. albicans.14,15 Nonetheless, as these nanoparticles are novel, the mechanical properties of this addition to resin composite have yet to be evaluated.

Light curing is performed by emitting a wavelength of light that reacts with the photo-initiators within the resin, triggering a chemical reaction that results in the hardening and bonding of the resin restorative biomaterial. This step ensures that the material has completed setting.16,17 The main light curing systems used in dentistry are QTH lights and LED lights. QTH light cure systems utilize a tungsten filament to generate a wide range in the light spectrum, which is then filtered to the specific wavelength necessary to cure dental composites. LED light cure systems use a semiconductor to create a narrow range in the light spectrum. This does not require filtering as it is already accurately set to trigger the photo-initiators in the resin.18 Both systems are effective at light curing, but their advantages and disadvantages are varied. QTH light cure units (LCU) generally require less maintenance and are less expensive than LED, however, they produce heat. This heat may damage the tooth or surrounding oral structures. LED LCU are more efficient, consume less-power, generate less heat, and are more shock and vibration resistant, making them safer for patients and suitable for portable use; however, they are typically more expensive than halogen LCU.16,19

For a resin composite restoration, a sufficient light cure is crucial in the longevity of the restoration. An unpolymerized resin composite will have weaker mechanical properties and will not withstand masticatory forces.16,[20], [21], [22] As a result of the variable interrelation among light, degree of conversion, polymerization, and fillers, questions are raised regarding the effect of inorganic filler content on light transmission through the resin-matrix of composites. Moreover, no literature currently exists on the effects of the light curing systems LED and QTH on the mechanical properties of BFC modified with zMgO NPs. In this study, we aimed to assess the compressive strength, flexural strength, and hardness of BFC modified with antimicrobial zMgO NPs compared to unmodified BFC when cured using LED and QTH LCU. The null hypothesis was that there will be no difference in the mechanical properties between the unmodified and modified composites.

## Methodology

### Ethical approval

An ethical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee at King Abdulaziz University, Faculty of Dentistry (#100-10-17).

### Study design

An overview for the study design can be seen in Figure 1. 180 samples of BFC were prepared and divided into 3 groups with 60 samples each: unmodified BFC group (control), BFC modified with 0.3% zMgO NPs, and BFC modified with 0.5% zMgO NPs. The samples in each respective group were randomized using a computer software program (Research Randomizer, Version 4.0, Social Psychology Network). 30 samples of each group underwent light curing using a QTH light cure, while the other 30 underwent curing using a LED light cure.
