### Materials preparation

Magnesium oxide nanoparticles were synthesized and coated with zein polymer purchased from Sigma Chemical Co. Ltd (St Louis, MO, USA).13 The Tetric Line 3M™ N-Bulk-Fill (Ivoclar Vivadent AG Tetric-N Line™ Zurich, Switzerland) was procured. All other chemicals and kits were purchased through Merck & Co.©, a biopharmaceutical distributer in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The nanowires were synthesized by reacting magnesium acetate (Mg (CH3COO)2) (CAS No. 142-72-3, Sigma Chemical Co. Ltd, St Louis, MO, USA) and urea (CH4N2O) (CAS No. 57-13-6, Sigma Chemical Co. Ltd, St Louis, MO, USA) with the microwave hydrothermal technique. A mixture of magnesium acetate and water (6.4 g/75 ml) were continuously stirred (30 min, 25°C) as drops of urea were added into the water (1.2 g/25 ml).23 The solution was sealed and maintained in a Teflon-lined autoclave (Teflon Lined Hydrothermal Autoclave, Techinstro Industries, Maharashtra, India) (15 min, 180°C) with a microwave furnace (Microwave Furnace MS3500, Energy Beam Sciences, East Granby, CT, USA) (1000 W). After completion and cooling, the products were filtered through distilled water, rinsed with ethanol (Saudi Pharmaceutical Industry, Sudair Industrial City, KSA), and dried (24 h, 60°C), after which they were calcinated (1 h, 600°C).13

0.02 g of zein was dissolved in a blend of ethanol and 0.1 NaOH solvent (93.7% (v/v)) (CAS No.1310-73-2, Sigma Chemical Co. Ltd, St Louis, MO, USA). At 10°C and 20 kHz frequency under 750W of ultrasonic shear (USSC Shear Logic Ultrasonic, Newport, CA, USA), a mixture of MgO and polyvinyl alcohol (Carolina Biological Supply Company, Burlington, NC, USA) were saturated by a drizzle of zein solution. The mixture then underwent magnetic stirring (Hei-PLATE Mix ‘n’ Heat Ultimate, Heidolph, Schwabach, Germany) at a rate of 500 rpm. Afterwards, the blend was centrifuged twice at a rate of 3,000 rpm (CLS6758 Corning® LSE™ Compact Centrifuges, Glendale, AR, USA) for the duration of 45min to obtain pure NPs and purge the excess polyvinyl alcohol. Ethanol was evaporated on a rotary evaporator by keeping the temperature of the water bath at around 35°C-40°C to obtain refined non-agglomerated nanoparticles. The supernatant was extracted and zMgO pellet was dispersed in 5 ml buffer (PluriSelect Life Science, Leipzig, Germany). 2% (w/v) of trehalose (Louis Francious Supplier, Marne-la-Vallée, France) was implemented into the mixture, after which the mixture was lyophilized (VirTis Bench Top Lyophilizer, SP Industries, Stone Ridge, NY, USA).

A blend of zein with polyvinyl alcohol (2:1 by weight) was prepared, after which the MgO nanoparticles were readied (4:1 by weight). The two mixtures of MgO with zein and polyvinyl alcohol were stirred for 30 minutes on a magnetic stirrer, after which the polyvinyl alcohol was volatilized, the mix centrifuged, and finally freeze-dried. The powder was milled for 24 h at 400 rpm using 10 silicon carbide balls (14 mm diameter) (High Energy Ball Mill Emax, RETSCH, GMBH, Haan, Germany). The obtained powder was annealed using the same microwave furnace from earlier for 2 h with a heating rate of 10°C/min, varying the temperature from 450°C to 900°C. Afterwards, the BFC was mixed manually in the dark with zMgO nanoparticles by weight using a highly accurate scale to 0.0001 g (Mettler Toledo™, Fischer Scientific, USA) resulting in specimens with 0.3% and 0.5% zMgO concentration.13

### Samples preparation

The composite specimens were prepared according to the manufacturers’ instructions, which complies with the ISO standards (ISO 4049).24 For the compressive strength and hardness test, cylindrical 4 × 6 mm Teflon mold was used. For the flexural strength, a rectangular 2 × 2 × 25 mm Teflon mold was used. While in the dark, the unmodified and modified composites were placed into the respective mold and pressed between polyester strips under static load on a glass slide. The composite resins were light-cured from a zero-distance per the manufacturer's instructions using an LED curing device (3M ESPE Elipar™) with a 10-mm internal diameter and 430-480 nm wavelength, or a QTH device Spectrum 800 (SP) (Dentsply™ DeTrey GmbH, Konstanz, Germany) with an 8-mm internal diameter and 400-500 nm wavelength for 20 seconds on each side. Appropriate light curing practice was implemented: prior to LCU use, the tip was checked for debris and cleaned, the active LCU tip was flat and pressed against the surface to maximize curing, and sufficient curing time was fulfilled. The light cure units were checked between each cure to ensure that sufficient light curing would be achieved, and appropriate light curing practices were employed. The specimens for the flexural strength tests were light cured for multiple cycles as the curing tip diameter was smaller than the specimen length. Curing of the other side after removal from the mold was done to ensure complete polymerization.

### Characterization

#### X-ray diffraction

The crystalline structure of the modified composite specimens was assessed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD; Rigaku, Ultima IV, Japan). The parameters were as follows: Cu-Kα X-ray radiation (λ = 1.542 A°) along a diffraction angle of 2θ range of 30°-80°.

#### Field emission scanning electron microscopy

An analysis of the surface morphology and distribution of the zMgO NPs was conducted using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM; JEOL JSM-7600F, JEOL Ltd. Tokyo, Japan) at 1,500X magnification with an acceleration voltage of 5 kV with the lower electron detector.

#### Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy was employed to inspect the test samples’ chemical properties. The FTIR array was observed by a FTIR type 8000 series Fourier transformation (Shimadzu Co., Japan) in the absorbance mode at 400-4000 cm-1.

### Conduction of tests

#### Compressive strength test

To perform the compressive strength test, a universal testing machine was used (Instron #5944, Instron 5000 Premier Testing Systems series, Instron® Mechanical Testing Systems, Massachusetts, USA). Samples were loaded onto a block held in place with a mounting jig, and a compressive load was applied over the surface of the composite disk at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min with a 50 kilonewton loading cell. The maximum point right before fracture of the disk was recorded in megapascal (MPa). The calculation of the compressive strength was done using the following formula (1):(1) F = P A

F = The compressive strength (MPa); P = Maximum load (or load until failure) to the composite (Newton) A = Cross section of the area of the composite disc (mm2).

#### Flexural strength test

To perform the flexural strength test, a universal testing machine was used (Instron #5944, Instron 5000 Premier Testing Systems series, Instron® Mechanical Testing Systems, Massachusetts, USA). Samples were loaded onto a block held in place with a mounting jig, and the arm of the machine applied a 3-point load at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min with a 50 kilonewton leading cell. The maximum point right before fracture of the specimen was recorded in megapascal (MPa). The calculation of the flexural strength was done using the following formula (2):(2) S = 3 F L 2 b d 2

S = the flexural strength (MPa); F = the maximum load applied to the composite specimen (Newton); L = the span in between the supports (20 mm); b and d are respectively the width and height of the composite specimen in mm.

#### Hardness test

The samples were subjected to a microhardness test using Vickers Hardness Machine (Micromet 6040, Buehler, USA) under a load of 100 g and dwell time of 10 seconds. Three readings were taken, and the average was recorded in Vickers Pyramid Number (HV) according to the formula (3):(3) H V = 1.854 F D 2

F = the applied load (measured in kilograms-force); D = the area of the indentation (measured in square millimetres).

### Statistical analysis

The data obtained (compressive strength, flexural strength, and hardness values) were collected and analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences software (SPSS) (Version 20.0, IBM, New York, USA). Shapiro–Wilk test was used to test for normality of data. Two-way ANOVA (between the control and the groups reinforced with different zMgO NPs concentrations and between the two light cure systems LED and QTH) and Tukey's post-hoc test was conducted at P = .05 to delineate areas of significance.

## Discussion

The mechanical properties of composite are affected by several vital factors, particularly the type and size of fillers, the degree of conversion of resin, and the curing conditions. The filler particles size and shape influence the composite's ability to withstand deformation and fracture.3,25 The degree of conversion refers to the percentage of resin molecules in the matrix that react to form the polymer network. Higher degrees of conversion will lead to composites with better mechanical properties but may also result in increased shrinkage during the light curing process. Furthermore, the curing conditions which involve time of exposure to the light, the intensity of the light, and the distance of the target from the light source can all affect the mechanical properties of the composite. Improper or incomplete curing will subsequently affect the longevity of the composite restoration, as it will be weaker and susceptible to deterioration over time.16,21

Recently, numerous studies exploring the usage of organic and inorganic nanoparticles as fillers in dental resin composite have emerged with results presenting that nanoparticles could ameliorate the properties of the resin composite.8,26 This study is part of a large project involving the investigation of zMgO NPs and their dental implications.[13], [14], [15], [27], [28], [29], [30], [31], [32] In this study, an assessment was conducted of the mechanical properties of unmodified and modified BFC with two different curing lights LED and QTH. The weight concentrations 0.3% and 0.5% were chosen as the lowest concentration that could still impart an antimicrobial effect onto the resin composite, as determined by previous studies.[13], [14], [15],30

Beyond the core components of the composite, several key factors must be followed to ensure complete and thorough curing of the composite and thereby ensure sufficient mechanical properties. The restorative material should correspond to the light curing system being used. Furthermore, the curing conditions must be monitored closely; that includes using the appropriate intensity, following the manufacturer's instructions regarding the curing time, and minimizing the distance between the light source and the target. Lastly, it is imperative to pause frequently while light curing as the process can generate heat, and rapid, continuous curing can lead to overheating and damaging the tooth and surrounding tissues.33,34

As zMgO NPs have only recently been introduced, characterization of this novel biomaterial is essential to form a more thorough understanding of its properties and characteristics. Characterization of the nanoparticles alone were done in an earlier study.13 The TEM images revealed that the nanowires were about 30-60 nm wide and 2-3 μm long, and the XRD profile demonstrated strong and sharp diffraction peaks located at 2θ values of 36.2°, 45.4° and 66.2° corresponding to the (111), (200) and (220) planes, respectively, indicating that the powders were highly crystalline.

The XRD profile of the hybrid material reveals the types of phases and the crystalline structures of the samples. The XRD spectra of the composite with and without the zMgO NPS presented with no definite diffraction peaks (Figure 2). This could be due to the amorphous structure of the composite polymer as well as the microscopic volume of the nanoparticles within the BFC samples. The FTIR spectroscopy can report on the chemical properties of the modified BFC when compared to the unmodified BFC. There was no significant change in the FTIR spectra, which reveals that the incorporation of the zMgO NPs did not alter the chemical properties of the BFC, and that the hybrid biomaterial behaves equivalently to its unmodified counterpart (Figure 3). The surface morphology of the BFC and the distribution of the zMgO NPs within it were assessed with the FESEM analysis. The micrograph revealed a uniform and homogeneous distribution of the zMgO NPs in the BFC matrix, which denotes the preservation of the nano-properties of the zMgO NPs (Figure 4).

Variably sized nanoparticles absorb visible light distinctly, which confers to the degree of polymerization. The wavelength of the scattered light is established by the size of the nanoparticles. Short wavelengths are scattered by small nanoparticles while long wavelengths are scattered by the larger nanoparticles, and large particles are capable of scattering more light than small particles. The degree of polymerization is directly influenced by the filler size and distribution.35,36

Compressive strength is the capacity of a material to withstand compressive forces, and it is an important property to assess in a dental restoration as the majority of masticatory forces are compressive.37,38 It has been reported that highly filled materials exhibit superior mechanical properties.39,40 According to the Oxford Handbook of Applied Dental Science, physiological and normal mastication force varies from 70-150 N.41,42 In this study, the maximum compressive forces that the composite specimens withstood were >200 N. The BFC specimens filled with 0.3% zMgO NPs whether cured by LED or QTH showed a statistically significant difference from the control in terms of compressive strength, while the other groups showed no significant change. This increase in compressive strength could be due to the increased amount of filler load, which in turn improved the compressive strength of the composite. It could also be related to the small size of the zMgO NPs, which helps them integrate into the composite matrix and fill the gaps between the interpolymeric chains.[10], [11], [12],43 Moreover, zMgO NPs have high surface energy, resulting in increased wettability and permitting close cross-linking between the BFC resin particles and the inorganic nanoparticles.30,44 As a result, the BFC is more coherent and resists degradation under compressive forces. Similarly, Swetha et al. and Hojati et al. both found that the addition 1% zinc oxide nanoparticles to resin composite raised the compressive strength of the hybrid dental material, while Barot et al. found that immobilized silver nanoparticles at concentrations of 1%, 5% and 7% were capable of enhancing the compressive strength of the resin composite.6,45,46

Conversely, Alpöz et al. demonstrated that the compressive strength of BFC restorative materials did not improve with the increase in polymerization time, and Rodrigues et al. reported that despite the correlation between the filler amount and compressive strength of composite, the results could vary according to the type of material.47,48 In this study, the reinforcement of the BFC with 0.5% zMgO NPs showed an increase in compressive strength that was not statistically significant. This could be explained as the increased degree of dispersion of the nanoparticles into the matrix might have impeded the scale of monomer conversion, which would've resulted in the ensnarement of unreacted monomers that would then act as plasticizers.49,50

Moreover, there was a statistically significant difference in the compressive strengths between the LED group and the QTH group. QTH LCU and LED LCU units do not give similar irradiance values due to the fundamental differences between the two equipment. The QTH LCU delivers light with a wider wavelength and emission spectrum (in this case, 400-500 nm) compared to the LED LCU (430-480 nm). Tetric N-Ceram Bulk-Fill contains the photo-initiators camphorquinone with an acyl phosphine oxide and their patented ‘Ivocerin,’ a dibenzoyl germanium derivative. Ivocerin features a higher absorption coefficient than camphorquinone, which provides an increased quantum efficiency, allowing for more rapid polymerization, a deeper depth of cure and a reduced yellowish effect of the amine group. The absorption spectrum is from 370-460 nm, with a maximum peak at 415 nm.16,51 The QTH LCU's emission spectrum more closely suited the BFC than the LED LCU, hence the significant difference in the compressive strengths between the two groups.20,52 As the compressive strength of the modified composite significantly increased, the null hypothesis was therefore rejected.

Flexural strength is defined as the stress a material can withstand by bending before failure. Due to the clinical circumstances of the restoration, the composite will be subjected to considerable flexural strength, and as such a high flexural strength is necessary to withstand masticatory forces without undergoing fracture.38 In this study, there was no statistically significant difference in flexural strength between the groups (Figure 6). These results are in accordance with studies detailing that composites cured with LED units have flexural characteristics comparable to those cured with QTH units.[53], [54], [55] The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) document #4049 states that the recommended and minimum acceptable flexural strength for resin composite is 80 MPa.24,56 The inorganic nanoparticles’ addition did not alter nor hinder the inherent flexural strength of the composite. This could be explained by the low quantity of nanoparticles contributing to the inorganic fillers. Several studies assessing nanoparticles-incorporated hybrid resin composite found a significant increase in the flexural strength as those studies involved the addition of inorganic nanoparticles with high weight concentrations of 10%-50%. However, there were also results in which the flexural strength decreased as a result of the increased concentration of nano-sized oxides interrupting the matrix wetting of the fillers. Furthermore, higher concentrations of nanoparticle inclusion are at risk for agglomeration issues, and the opacity of the metal NPs can drastically reduce the curing depth.49 The difference in the results of the compressive and flexural tests can be due to the difference in the thickness of the samples affecting the polymerization, hence influencing the composites’ properties.

Microhardness is an indirect measure of the degree of conversion of a material, and can reveal information on the depth of polymerization, the polishability of the material and its abrasion resistance.57,58 The microhardness values of the modified composite increased slightly when compared to the unmodified composite for both the QTH and LED group, however, there was no statistically significant difference between the groups (Figure 7). This can be explained by the key feature of nanoparticles having an exceptionally large surface area to volume ratio. That large surface area gives the zMgO NPs the capacity to integrate more contact within the composite matrix, structurally fortifying the composite as a whole.5,11 However, due to the small amount of the nanoparticles incorporated, the reinforcement was not enough to create a significant effect. Furthermore, it's important to note the relationship between the degree of conversion that the composite undergoes and its microhardness. LED LCU's that are not uniform in their light emission will negatively affect the microhardness of the final resin restoration.59,60 Additionally, it was found that higher quantities of inorganic nanoparticles could leave undissolved monomers, leading to less cross-linking and subsequently reduced microhardness. Jafary et al. tested the microhardness of resin composite incorporated with titanium oxide nanoparticles and found that microhardness significantly increased at 1% concentration, did not significantly change at 2% concentration and significantly decreased at 3% concentration.49,61

The efficacy of the light curing is affected by the type of composite material, the thickness of the material, the location of the tooth cavity and operator factors. In particular, the intensity of the light is a critical component. Higher intensity lights can cure composites faster, but at the risk of generating more heat and causing more shrinkage, which in turn can lead to gaps and subsequently microleakage.16 Typically, LED light cure systems are more popular due to their precision and efficiency as they emit larger amounts of light in the area of 470 nm. Halogen lights used to be the most commonly utilized LCU in dentistry. They are preferred when the composite material being used is not reactive to LED light, or when curing materials contain multiple photo-initiators, which would require the broader spectrum of light that halogen light systems are capable of.22

The literature demonstrates divided opinions regarding the efficacy of LED versus QTH. Several studies reported that LEDs were found to be more successful than the halogen units with respect to curing depth or microhardness properties, while other studies determined that QTH was superior or that both were the equal in efficacy.62,63 Choudhary et al. demonstrated that curing nano-composites with QTH resulted in better surface hardness while curing micro-hybrid composites with QTH and LED resulted in comparable surface hardness.64 The division in the literature could be a result of differences in the wavelength spectrum, energy density, intensity of the LCU, spectral distribution, photo-initiators and manufacturer variability used in the utilized composite resin.65

The limitations of the study involve the challenge in completely simulating the intraoral conditions. Consistent static, chemical, and cyclic mechanical fatigue on the composite restorations were not replicated. Further dynamic loading in artificial saliva before testing may more closely simulate intraoral conditions when considering the hydrolytic degradation of the bond due to pH changes of saliva. Additionally, thermocycling can be implemented to assess the effects of thermal degradation on the modified composites. Moreover, it should be noted that as the BFC was mixed manually, this may have led to inconsistencies in the mixing procedure.

## Conclusion

This study established that the mechanical properties of compressive strength, flexural strength, and hardness will not be hindered by the modification of antimicrobial zMgO NPs to Tetric N-Ceram bulk-fill composite. The modified hybrid composite retained its mechanical properties while exhibiting an antimicrobial effect imparted by the inorganic nanoparticles, thereby improving as a dental restoration. Long-term clinical studies can further substantiate the enhanced resin composite.
